brief: A ZeroHedge write-up of Goldman Sachs' 'The Macro Call' with Mark Wilson, Jan Scheffel and George Cole, including a transcript the note states is reconstructed and non verbatim. The argument: AI has stopped being only an equity story and is becoming a rates-and-credit story. AI infrastructure needs very large upfront capital, that capital is increasingly raised as long-dated debt, AI-related issuance had approached $500 billion by early August or roughly one-fifth of 2026 US high-grade supply, and funding next year's $1.3TN of capex means the hyperscaler complex issues more DV01 than the US Treasury. Buyers must then reallocate out of Treasuries and mortgages, which can lift credit spreads, real yields and the term premium, while the boom raises capital demand and possibly the neutral rate before productivity arrives. Cole qualifies that AI issuance is a contributor and not the sole explanation, with government deficits, energy inflation, hawkish central banks and European fiscal politics also driving yields. Wilson's framing is that the Fed is more passenger than driver. The funding gets done but the cost of capital is the new constraint, and they report no signs yet of offsetting AI productivity apart from falling token costs.
